records.stem: Explain the meaning of a subsidy.
records.context: Table 1 Government subsidies to some Namibian State Owned Enterprises (SOEs) and institutions GOVERNMENT SUBSIDIES (N$) 2016/17 2017/18 (millions) 2018/19 (millions) Air Namibia 695 million 486 494 TransNamib 313 million 220 213 NSFAF (Namibian Student Financial Assistance Fund) 1,2 billion 962 950 UNAM (University of Namibia) 999 million 926 919 NUST (National University of Science and Technology) 482 million 533 522 Namibia Training Authority 509 million 392 400 Namibian State Owned Enterprises (SOEs) and institutions felt the effect of the tightening state budget since 2016/17.  Despite the lower amount of subsidies, SOEs and government institutions were still allocated about N$4,6 billion from the state budget in 2017/18.  At N$4,6 billion, government subsidies to SOEs in 2017/18 was N$1,8 billion less than in 2016/17. Air Namibia, as a loss-making national airline, has received financial lifelines totalling N$4,2 billion from the government over the past seven financial years, from 2010/11 to 2016/17. Two thirds of the total amount of subsidies were allocated to higher education institutions such as NUST and UNAM.  Higher education received 65% of the subsidies that government would have given to other SOEs and other state- supported institutions. Critics of SOEs often argue for a privatisation of loss-making enterprises.  The government though, believes that privatisation may cause more problems than it solves, resulting in more corruption, a greater rich-poor divide, increased social tensions, and enriching only a select few.  SOEs are assets of enormous value to the state and thus the citizens of the country.  Abusiness such as NamPower, apart from the potentially large future earnings, has a significant amount of land, buildings, equipment, and other physical assets.  To privatise such a firm it must be ensured that the business is sold at a fair price and it also needs to find a way, throughservicecontracts,orthroughregulation,toensurethebusinesscontinues to provide affordable services to all citizens. (Adapted: Namibian March 2017)

records.stem: Describe how division of labour leads to specialisation. Support your answer with examples from the extract.
records.context: In 2019 thatch grass vendors in the Kavango region of Namibia used division of labour to specialise in the harvesting, bundle-making and selling of thatch grass as their main source of income. Although the demand for the grass outstripped the supply of the grass, the vendors were not able to increase the supply of thatch grass, due to not having advanced harvesting machinery and tools.  Since the thatch grass market was not regulated, buyers could decide on the price that they were willing to pay per bundle.  The buyers then sold the grass at much higher prices to businesses such as lodges and hotels.  These were some of the biggest markets that used the thatch grass for roofs.  In 2020, due to the six-month long Covid-19 imposed state of emergency, the tourism and construction industries in Namibia were affected very badly and the vendors of thatch grass faced possible closure as there was no market for their product. (Adapted article from The Namibian, 13 October 2020)

records.stem: Explain the form of business organisation of the berry farming business.
